turns.speaker: A
turns.text: If you open a fine watch and look at the main plate, you may see a pattern of small overlapping circles, like fish scales or bubbles. This decoration is called perlage. In English, it is sometimes called circular graining.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Perlage is made with a small rotating peg, usually tipped with an abrasive material. The craftsperson presses the spinning peg onto the metal for a moment, creating one tiny circle. Then the plate is moved slightly, and the next circle is made, partly covering the first one. Row by row, the pattern spreads across the surface.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: It sounds simple, but even spacing is essential. If the circles are not regular, the eye notices immediately. On a high-quality piece, the pattern looks smooth and calm, with soft reflections that change as the watch moves.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Interestingly, perlage is often found on surfaces most people never see, such as the dial side of the baseplate, under the dial. This shows that it began as a sign of care, not as marketing. Some people also say the tiny textures helped catch small particles of dust, although this is hard to prove.

turns.speaker: A
turns.text: Today, perlage can be made by machines as well as by hand. Still, it remains one of the classic finishes in watchmaking. When a maker decorates even hidden parts, it suggests that the visible parts have received the same attention.
